newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Burundian rebel leader states conditions for peace.
newsitem.headline: Burundian rebel leader states conditions for peace.

text.p: The militant opposition group fighting to oust Burundi's military government headed by Major Pierre Buyoya said on Tuesday it would only talk about a ceasefire if the rule of law and democracy were restored first.

"It is out of the question to negotiate a ceasefire until these two conditions have been accepted," Christian Sendegeya, vice president of the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD), told a news conference.
The majority Hutu CNDD's fighting wing, the Forces for the Defence of Democracy (FDD), have been waging a guerilla war against the Tutsi-dominated government and army for more than three years.

Buyoya, president of Burundi between 1988 and 1993 when he lost the country's first national elections, was reinstalled by the army in a coup on July 25 this year as ethnic violence ran amok, killing an estimated 1,000 a month.
The landlocked country has since been sealed off from the outside world by land and air trade and transport embargoes.

U.S. envoy Howard Wolpe is currently on a tour of the region as an advance scout for Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who will meet some of the key pro-sanctions African presidents in Arusha, Tanzania, on October 11.
A regional summit on Burundi is planned for October 12 in Arusha.

African diplomatic sources said the United States might hope to arrange a breakthrough meeting between Buyoya and CNDD president Leonard Nyangoma, with Christopher in attendance and the U.S. taking much of the credit, during that summit.
The pressure to make peace with Nyangoma is rising steadily. Hutus are 85 percent of Burundi's six million population and there is broad support for the rebels, described as "terrorists" by the army.
Large parts of the country are no-go areas. Main roads are potential death-traps from ambushes against soldiers and Tutsis, leading to heavy reprisals by the army.
In Brussels, Sendegeya said Burundi virtually had dual administrations, with CNDD supporters having elected governors in each province and local representatives beneath them.
He did not elaborate on how the elections had been conducted.
